purpose: Fixed corpus shared by BOTH fingerprint implementations (Java PackFingerprint and the PowerShell port). A cross-implementation test that each side feeds from its own copy would drift; both sides read THIS file.
rules: Every 'expect' here was derived BY REASONING from the Java rule text, never produced by running either implementation. A corpus whose expected values were generated by one side can only prove that side agrees with itself.

The authoritative rule (PackFingerprint.normalizeForDigest): only when relPath ends with '.properties' (case-insensitive), remove every occurrence of (?m)^#\w{3} \w{3} \d{2} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2} \w+ \d{4}\R? ; otherwise return the text unchanged.

Java defaults apply: \w = [A-Za-z0-9_] (ASCII), \d = [0-9] (ASCII), \R = \u000D\u000A | [\u000A\u000B\u000C\u000D\u0085\u2028\u2029], and (?m)^ matches at the start of input and after a Java line terminator (\n, \r, \r\n, \u0085, \u2028, \u2029).
NOTE: VT (\u000B) and FF (\u000C) are members of \R but are NOT line terminators for ^ in Java.
The digest is sha256Prefix16(normalized) = the first 16 lowercase hex characters of SHA-256 over the UTF-8 bytes of the NORMALIZED TEXT (not the file bytes).

cases.why: Real Iris/Oculus patch output. Its first line is the java.util.Properties.store() date header, which every round rewrites. After that line the three sampled files are byte-identical (verified on disk).
cases.trap: This is the case the whole normalization exists for: normalized digests must be equal across rounds while raw digests differ.

cases.why: Same file from the sibling slot: 31,934 B, identical after line 1, header differs only in the timestamp.
cases.trap: Second independent round; equality with A1 is the real claim.

cases.why: An archived copy from an earlier round (docs/evidence/2026-09-27-fingerprint-verify/run1-block.properties), third distinct timestamp.
cases.trap: Three-way equality makes 'same package, N rounds' a measurement rather than a two-point coincidence.

cases.why: Canonical header followed by LF: the trailing \R? consumes the LF together with the header.
cases.trap: Baseline positive.

cases.why: Real files are CRLF; \R matches \r\n as one unit and it is consumed with the header.
cases.trap: A port that splits on \n only would leave a stray \r behind.

cases.why: A lone CR is a member of \R, so it is consumed with the header.
cases.trap: Lone-CR files are unusual but the rule covers them.

cases.why: \R? is optional, so a header at EOF with no terminator still matches; the result is the empty string.
cases.trap: A port that requires a terminator is wrong.

cases.why: Both header lines match independently and both are removed.
cases.trap: replaceAll is global, not first-match-only.

cases.why: store() pads single-digit days with a space: '#Thu Jan  1 ...' has TWO spaces before the day. \w{3} consumes 'Jan', the literal space consumes the first space, then \d{2} must match ' 1' ... which it CANNOT (a space is not a digit). So this line does NOT match and is returned unchanged.
cases.trap: TRAP DISARMED: I first WROTE the expectation as a strip (and the port caught it): the rule text says otherwise. This documents that space-padded days are NOT normalized -- see B10 for the zero-padded contrast.

cases.why: Zero-padded day ('01') DOES satisfy \d{2}, so this header is stripped.
cases.trap: Contrast with B6: the rule strips only the zero-padded form, which is a REAL LIMITATION, because java.util.Properties.store() space-pads days 1-9. On those days the header survives normalization and the digest still drifts.

cases.why: The extension test is case-insensitive (toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).endsWith(".properties")).
cases.trap: A case-sensitive EndsWith would leave this file unnormalized.

cases.why: CONTROL: identical content, non-.properties path. normalizeForDigest returns the text untouched, so a .fsh whose only change is a date-header-looking line still yields a different digest.
cases.trap: Stripping '^#' lines in GLSL would erase real #version/#define content and manufacture false stability.

cases.why: The suffix must be exactly '.properties'.
cases.trap: A 'contains .properties' test would be too wide.

cases.why: One-digit day: \d{2} needs two digits.
cases.trap: Near miss; must NOT strip.

cases.why: Seconds missing: the pattern requires HH:MM:SS.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: Time zone missing: after HH:MM:SS the pattern needs \w+ then a space then \d{4}, which '2026' alone cannot satisfy.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: Two-digit year: \d{4} needs four.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: No leading '#': the pattern starts with a literal '#'.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: '#' not at a line start: ^ anchors the match.
cases.trap: A port that drops the anchor would strip mid-line.

cases.why: Weekday too long: \w{3} consumes 'Sat', then a literal space is required but 'u' follows.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: The '#' is inside a value, not at a line start.
cases.trap: Near miss.

cases.why: '#define FOO 1': after 'def' the pattern needs a space then three word chars then a space then two digits; 'ine' + space + 'FO' fails the digit test.
cases.trap: GLSL-style lines inside a .properties file must survive.

cases.why: DOCUMENTED POSITIVE: the rule is case-agnostic (\w covers lowercase), so a lowercase header IS stripped.
cases.trap: Listed to stop someone 'fixing' this into a near miss: it is correct behaviour, not a bug.

cases.why: Trailing space: the match ends after the four-digit year and \R? cannot consume a space, so the matched part is removed and the space plus newline REMAIN.
cases.trap: Documents that the result is not always 'the whole line disappears'.

cases.why: KILLER (non-ASCII letter): Java's \w is ASCII, so 'M\u00e4r' cannot match \w{3}. A .NET-naive \w (Unicode) WOULD match and strip.
cases.trap: Acceptance evidence for writing [A-Za-z0-9_] explicitly.

cases.why: KILLER: same class as D1, different position/letter.
cases.trap: Two samples of the same divergence make an accidental pass less likely.

cases.why: KILLER (non-ASCII digits): Java's \d is ASCII, so Arabic-Indic digits cannot satisfy \d{4}. A .NET-naive \d (Unicode) WOULD match.
cases.trap: Acceptance evidence for writing [0-9] explicitly.

cases.why: KILLER: non-ASCII digits in the hour.
cases.trap: Same class as D3, different field.

cases.why: KILLER (?m line terminators): Java's ^ matches after a lone CR, so the second header IS stripped. .NET's (?m)^ only matches after \n, so a port relying on it would not strip.
cases.trap: Acceptance evidence for emulating Java's ^ instead of using .NET (?m).

cases.why: KILLER: U+2028 (LINE SEPARATOR) is a Java line terminator for ^, so the header after it is stripped.
cases.trap: Same divergence class as D5.

cases.why: Five-digit year: the pattern has NO trailing anchor, so it consumes exactly four digits and leaves the fifth plus the newline.
cases.trap: Documents a genuine fragility: adding a '$' anchor would change this. Listed so the behaviour is pinned rather than discovered later.

cases.why: VT (U+000B) is a member of Java's \R, so it is consumed with the header.
cases.trap: Acceptance evidence that the port's terminator class must include \u000B; a class of \r\n|[\n\r\u0085\u2028\u2029] omits it and diverges here.

cases.why: FF (U+000C) is also a member of Java's \R.
cases.trap: Acceptance evidence for \u000C in the terminator class.

cases.why: NEL (U+0085) is a Java line terminator for ^ (and a \R member), so the header after it is stripped.
cases.trap: Completes the line-terminator coverage beyond D5/D6.
